cards.front: Recall a key point about Seasons & Orbital Mechanics
cards.back: The seasons are caused by the Earth's axial tilt of 23.5° relative to its orbital plane, NOT by the Earth's distance from the Sun.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Seasons & Orbital Mechanics
cards.back: In summer (northern hemisphere): the North Pole tilts toward the Sun, giving longer days, higher solar altitude, and more concentrated insolation.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Seasons & Orbital Mechanics
cards.back: In winter (northern hemisphere): the North Pole tilts away from the Sun, giving shorter days, lower solar altitude, and less concentrated insolation.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Seasons & Orbital Mechanics
cards.back: The summer solstice (~21 June): the Sun is directly overhead at the Tropic of Cancer (23.5°N); longest day in the northern hemisphere.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Seasons & Orbital Mechanics
cards.back: The winter solstice (~21 December): the Sun is directly overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn (23.5°S); shortest day in the northern hemisphere.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Seasons & Orbital Mechanics
cards.back: The equinoxes (~21 March and ~23 September): the Sun is directly overhead at the equator; day and night are approximately equal everywhere.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Seasons & Orbital Mechanics
cards.back: The Earth's orbit is slightly elliptical (eccentricity ~0.017): perihelion (closest, ~147 million km) occurs around 3 January; aphelion (farthest, ~152 million km) around 4 July.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Seasons & Orbital Mechanics
cards.back: The Earth is actually closest to the Sun during the northern hemisphere winter, confirming that distance does NOT cause the seasons.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Seasons & Orbital Mechanics
cards.back: The apparent path of the Sun against the background stars is called the ecliptic; it passes through the 12 zodiac constellations over the year.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Seasons & Orbital Mechanics
cards.back: Precession of the equinoxes: the Earth's axis slowly wobbles over a 26,000-year cycle, changing which stars are at the celestial poles and shifting the zodiac signs over millennia.

cards.front: What should you know about gcse astronomy exam tips — seasons & orbital mechanics?
cards.back: 1. For Seasons & Orbital Mechanics questions, define key terms before explaining processes 2. Use 'because' to link cause and effect in your explanations 3.
